headline: Connecticut raises standard rebate for new battery-electric vehicles to $1,500
dek: The CHEAPR increase takes effect Oct. 15, while additional rebates remain available for income-qualified buyers and residents of environmental-justice communities.
body: Connecticut is increasing the standard point-of-sale rebate for a new battery-electric vehicle from $1,000 to $1,500 on Thursday, a change state officials say is intended to lower the upfront cost of cleaner transportation as buyers face higher vehicle prices and the loss of a federal incentive. The Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection announced the change Oct. 14 for the Connecticut Hydrogen and Electric Automobile Purchase Rebate, known as CHEAPR.

The higher amount applies to an eligible vehicle purchased or leased on or after Oct. 15, according to DEEP. The standard program is open to Connecticut licensed drivers who buy or lease an eligible new vehicle from a licensed Connecticut new-car dealer or an eligible original equipment manufacturer. DEEP’s program materials set a $50,000 price cap for new vehicles and describe the standard rebate as a point-of-sale credit, meaning the approved amount is applied through the purchase or lease transaction rather than handled as a later state tax filing.

The increase does not change every CHEAPR incentive. The standard rebate for a new plug-in hybrid remains $500. For buyers who qualify for Rebate+, the additional voucher for a new battery-electric vehicle remains $3,000, bringing the combined new-BEV incentive to $4,500. The Rebate+ add-on for a new plug-in hybrid remains $1,500, for a combined $2,000. Rebate+ incentives for used vehicles also remain unchanged at $5,000 for a battery-electric vehicle and $3,000 for a plug-in hybrid, according to DEEP’s updated program page.

Rebate+ is targeted rather than automatic. A Connecticut driver must be prequalified and meet at least one of the program’s criteria: living in an environmental-justice community or distressed municipality, participating in a qualifying state or federal income-support program, or having household income below 300% of the federal poverty level. The [CHEAPR Rebate+ guidance](https://portal.ct.gov/deep/air/mobile-sources/cheapr/cheapr---rebate-plus) says people seeking the new-vehicle add-on must apply for a voucher before buying or leasing and provide that voucher to the dealer. Private sales are not eligible for the used-vehicle Rebate+ incentive.

DEEP said the policy is a response to a sharp change in the electric-vehicle market. Demand for CHEAPR surged in 2025 before the federal tax credit expired on Oct. 1 of that year, prompting the state to reduce its standard rebate. The agency said rebates have fallen by half since the federal credit ended and pointed to tariffs, manufacturing costs and vehicle availability as additional pressures. Returning the standard new-BEV amount to $1,500 is meant to narrow that affordability gap, although it does not restore the larger federal benefit that Connecticut buyers previously could have combined with state help.

The program is already a statewide transportation and air-quality policy, not just a discount for early adopters. DEEP said CHEAPR has helped almost 28,000 drivers obtain an electric vehicle and issued more than $50 million in rebates since the program began in 2015. The department also reported more than 2,700 new-EV incentives since the start of 2026, including more than 520 Rebate+ awards. The [Center for Sustainable Energy](https://energycenter.org/program/connecticut-hydrogen-and-electric-automobile-purchase-rebate-program), which administers CHEAPR, describes it as the nation’s first statewide point-of-sale EV rebate program and reported nearly $48.7 million in issued or reserved rebates as of April 2026; the different totals reflect different reporting dates and program accounting.

The stakes reach beyond the transaction at a dealership. DEEP says Connecticut has more than 2.7 million registered vehicles, with cars and trucks responsible for almost 70% of smog-forming emissions and nearly 35% of the state’s climate pollution. The agency reported that Connecticut’s air exceeded federal ozone standards on 17 days in 2026, compared with 22 days in 2025 and 23 days in 2024. Those figures are the department’s rationale for treating vehicle incentives as an air-quality tool, while the immediate household benefit depends on the price, financing, charging access and operating needs of each vehicle buyer.

For residents considering a purchase, the practical sequence is to confirm that the vehicle appears on the current CHEAPR eligible list, ask the dealer to process the standard rebate, and complete Rebate+ prequalification before signing if the household may qualify. The U.S. Department of Energy’s [Alternative Fuels Data Center](https://afdc.energy.gov/laws/all?state=CT) says CHEAPR awards are first-come, first-served. DEEP said it will continue monitoring demand and work with the CHEAPR board and General Assembly on future program changes, so the amounts and available funding remain subject to later state decisions.
